rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window while limiting the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Lengthen only the gradient to test whether the early critical pair responds to slope. The last peak should remain near or below 10 minutes, allowing improved resolution without a substantial time penalty.

The critical early pair improved only slightly with a shallower gradient, suggesting temperature is a more promising selectivity lever. Raise temperature while keeping the gradient fixed to measure that effect and shorten retention.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; now test a shorter gradient to reduce analysis time while retaining full resolution. Keep temperature and solvent endpoints fixed to isolate the effect of gradient steepness.
Narrow the gradient window to recover resolution of the first pair with a slope between injections 3 and 4. This should retain the maximum CRF while eluting the last peak sooner than injection 3.

Shift the solvent window upward while preserving injection 5’s gradient slope to test whether initial solvent strength can shorten retention without losing critical-pair resolution. Injection 5 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

Test the low-temperature selectivity regime with a shorter gradient: the early pair may separate on the opposite side of a temperature-driven elution-order crossover. The broad solvent window should still elute all compounds promptly, while injection 5 remains the fully resolved fallback.

Raise temperature one step from injection 7 to split the late three-peak cluster while testing whether the early pair remains fully resolved. Keeping the gradient fixed isolates this selectivity trade-off.

Use a slope between the fully resolved injection 5 and slightly under-resolved injection 4, targeting full resolution in less time. The final peak may elute during the hold, but the previous high-temperature runs suggest this endpoint is close to its elution strength.

Explore an intermediate temperature to separate the late cluster seen at 30 C, with a higher starting organic fraction to shorten the run and test early-pair selectivity. Injection 9 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Test whether a shallower gradient resolves the early pair at 35 C while preserving separation of the later cluster. Keeping the solvent endpoints fixed isolates slope sensitivity in this alternative selectivity regime.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 9 to locate the fastest fully resolved boundary at 60 C. The critical pair is close to R = 1.5, so this small change may shorten retention but risks a slight resolution loss.

Test whether a higher initial organic fraction changes early-pair selectivity enough to enable a faster fully resolved method at 35 C. The shallower slope should help preserve separation of the later cluster, while injection 9 remains the best time-saving fallback.

Reduce the slope relative to injection 6 to recover early-pair resolution while retaining its shorter initial retention. This tests whether a shifted, shallower window offers a competitive fully resolved method with more resolution margin than injection 9.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a shallower gradient for greater critical-pair resolution margin. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, potentially preserving CRF 1.000 with less sensitivity to small method variations.

Test whether a much steeper gradient breaks the late three-peak coincidence observed at 25 C through slope-dependent selectivity. This could reveal a substantially faster fully resolved regime; injection 9 remains the established fallback.

Refine around the fastest fully resolved method using a slightly shallower slope and an endpoint high enough to keep the last peak inside the gradient. This should preserve CRF 1.000 with a little more early-pair resolution margin and a last peak near 7 minutes.

Test a shallower gradient to increase the early-pair resolution margin while monitoring the narrowing third-to-fourth peak separation. The last peak is expected before 10 minutes, so this may provide another maximum-score method with better balanced resolution.

Shift injection 18’s solvent window upward while preserving its slope to shorten retention and improve the third-to-fourth peak separation. The early pair should retain enough resolution margin to preserve the maximum CRF.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 14 to shorten retention while keeping the early pair near baseline resolution. This refines the full-resolution boundary for the 0.10 starting organic fraction without risking a low-strength final hold.

Refine between injections 15 and 18 to balance the two limiting early pairs while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. Maximum CRF is already secured; this tests a method with greater resolution margin than the fastest fully resolved injection 9.

Trim injection 3’s upper solvent window while preserving its successful gradient slope. This should retain full resolution and CRF 1.000 with a shorter programmed gradient, providing an alternative with more resolution margin than injection 9.

Shorten the programmed gradient relative to injection 14 while making its slope slightly shallower to preserve early-pair resolution. The final peak should remain inside the gradient, yielding another compact maximum-CRF candidate without a low-strength hold.

Preserve injection 22’s fully resolving slope while trimming the programmed gradient to 8 minutes. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution strength, so this should retain CRF 1.000 and its resolution margin without extending retention.

Use the final injection to test a compact gradient with slightly more resolution margin than injection 24, targeting full resolution and a last peak near 8 minutes. The maximum CRF is already secured, with injection 9 remaining the fastest fully resolved method tested.
